Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

sift

Recursive search for the impatient.
Guide · FAQ · Changelog

[![CI](https://github.com/acme-tools/sift/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg?branch=main)](https://github.com/acme-tools/sift/actions/workflows/ci.yml?query=branch%3Amain) [![crates.io](https://img.shields.io/crates/v/sift-search.svg?logo=rust)](https://crates.io/crates/sift-search) [![docs.rs](https://img.shields.io/docsrs/sift-search)](https://docs.rs/sift-search) [![License: MIT OR Apache-2.0](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT%20OR%20Apache--2.0-blue.svg)](#license) [![MSRV](https://img.shields.io/badge/rustc-1.74+-lightgray.svg)](https://blog.rust-lang.org/2023/11/16/Rust-1.74.0.html) [![Packaging status](https://repology.org/badge/tiny-repos/sift-search.svg)](https://repology.org/project/sift-search/versions) [![Downloads](https://img.shields.io/crates/d/sift-search?label=downloads&style=flat-square)](https://crates.io/crates/sift-search) `sift` is a line-oriented search tool that recursively searches the current directory for a regex pattern. It respects your `.gitignore`, skips hidden files and binaries by default, and is usually *at least* as fast as whatever you're using now. Think of it as `grep -r` with better defaults and nicer output — it is not a drop-in replacement and doesn't try to be POSIX-compliant. > **sift is in maintenance mode for the 1.x series.** Bug fixes still land, new features go into the `2.0` branch. See [#412](https://github.com/acme-tools/sift/issues/412) for the plan. ## Table of contents - [Features](#features) - [Installation](#installation) - [Usage](#usage) - [Configuration](#configuration) - [Benchmarks](#benchmarks) - [FAQ](#faq) - [License](#license) ## Features - **Fast by default** — SIMD-accelerated literal search plus a parallel directory walker. - falls back to a plain `memchr` loop on CPUs without AVX2/NEON - memory-maps large files when that is actually faster (rarely, it turns out) - **Respects ignore files**: `.gitignore`, `.ignore`, `.siftignore` and your global git excludes - `-u` turns this off, `-uu` also searches hidden files, `-uuu` searches binaries too - **Smart case** — a pattern with no uppercase letters is matched case-insensitively - **Multiline mode** with `-U`, so `\n` in a pattern just works - **File types**: `-t py`, `-T js`, or define your own with `--type-add 'proto:*.proto'` - **JSON output** (`--json`), one object per line, documented in [docs/json.md][json-docs] - **Preprocessors** - built-in decompression for `.gz`, `.bz2`, `.xz`, `.lz4` and `.zst` (`-z`) - arbitrary commands via `--pre`, e.g. `--pre pdftotext` for PDFs ## Installation ## Binaries are published for Linux, macOS and Windows on every tagged release. Pick whatever is easiest: 1. **Homebrew** (macOS and Linux) ```sh brew install acme-tools/tap/sift ``` 2. **Cargo** — requires Rust 1.74 or newer: ```sh cargo install sift-search --locked ``` The crate is called `sift-search` because `sift` was already taken on crates.io,[^name] but the installed binary is just `sift`. 3. **Scoop** / **Winget** (Windows) ```powershell scoop bucket add acme https://github.com/acme-tools/scoop-bucket scoop install sift # or, if you prefer winget winget install --id AcmeTools.Sift -e ``` 4. **Pre-built archives** from the [releases page][releases]: - Linux - `x86_64-unknown-linux-musl` — static, runs on basically anything - `aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu` — Raspberry Pi 4/5, Graviton - macOS: one universal binary (`sift--universal-apple-darwin.tar.gz`) - Windows: `sift--x86_64-pc-windows-msvc.zip` Every archive has a `.sha256` file next to it: ```console $ sha256sum -c sift-1.8.2-x86_64-unknown-linux-musl.tar.gz.sha256 sift-1.8.2-x86_64-unknown-linux-musl.tar.gz: OK ``` 5. **From source** ```sh git clone https://github.com/acme-tools/sift.git cd sift cargo build --release --features pcre2 # pcre2 is optional ./target/release/sift --version ``` Distro packages exist for Arch (`pacman -S sift`), Alpine (`apk add sift`) and NixOS; they're maintained by volunteers, so they may lag behind a release or two. ## Usage ## ```console $ sift 'fn main' src/ src/main.rs 14:fn main() -> ExitCode { $ sift -t rust -w unwrap --stats crates/core/src/walk.rs 88: let meta = entry.metadata().unwrap(); 1 matches 1 matched lines 1 files contained matches 212 files searched 0.021 seconds ``` Patterns use Rust's [regex syntax](https://docs.rs/regex/latest/regex/#syntax), which is roughly Perl-style minus look-around and backreferences; if you need those, build with `--features pcre2` and pass `-P`, but be aware that the PCRE2 engine can be dramatically slower on pathological patterns and doesn't get the literal-prefix optimizations, so `sift -P '(?<=foo)bar'` over a large monorepo might take seconds instead of milliseconds. Patterns are matched line by line unless `-U` is given, and `sift` never searches files it considers binary unless you ask it to with `--binary` or `-uuu` (a file counts as binary if a NUL byte shows up in its first 8 KiB). Flags you will probably use every day: ```text -i / -s / -S ignore case / case sensitive / smart case (default) -w match whole words only -F treat the pattern as a literal string -l print only the names of matching files -C NUM show NUM lines of context --hidden search hidden files and directories -g '!*.min.js' exclude by glob (repeatable) ``` ### Configuration ### `sift` reads an optional config file from `$SIFT_CONFIG_PATH`. Each line is one argument, exactly as you'd type it on the command line; lines starting with `#` are ignored. | Flag | Env var | Default | What it does | |:-----|:-------:|--------:|:-------------| | `--threads ` | `SIFT_THREADS` | `0` | Number of search threads. `0` means "pick something sensible", which is the number of logical cores capped at 12 — past that point the directory walker, not the matcher, becomes the bottleneck on most SSDs. | | `--max-filesize ` | — | *none* | Skip files bigger than `SIZE`; accepts suffixes like `512K`, `10M`, `1G`. | | `-e, --regexp ` | — | — | Add a pattern; repeatable. `-e foo -e bar` is the same as `'foo\|bar'`. | | `--colors ` | `SIFT_COLORS` | see `sift --help` | e.g. `match:fg:magenta`, `path:style:bold`. Set `NO_COLOR=1` to turn color off entirely. | | `--sort ` | | `none` | `path`, `modified`, `accessed` or `created`. Sorting disables parallelism, so it is noticeably slower on big trees. | | `--json` | | `false` | Emit [JSON Lines](https://jsonlines.org/) instead of human-readable output. |
Shell completions Completion scripts ship in every release archive under `complete/`. You can also generate them yourself: * **bash** — `sift --generate complete-bash > ~/.local/share/bash-completion/completions/sift` * **zsh** — put `complete/_sift` somewhere on your `$fpath`, then run `compinit` * **fish**: ```fish sift --generate complete-fish > ~/.config/fish/completions/sift.fish ``` * **PowerShell** — add this to your `$PROFILE`: ```powershell sift --generate complete-powershell | Out-String | Invoke-Expression ```
### Benchmarks ### Searching a checkout of the Linux kernel (v6.8, ~1.4 GB, warm page cache).[^bench] Lower is better; don't read too much into differences under 10%. Tool | Command | Median | Matches ---|---|---|--- sift 1.8.2 | `sift -n PM_RESUME` | **0.118 s** | 17 ripgrep 14.1.0 | `rg -n PM_RESUME` | 0.121 s | 17 GNU grep 3.11 | `grep -rn PM_RESUME .` | 0.884 s | 17 git grep (2.44) | `git grep -n PM_RESUME`|0.310 s|17 ag 2.2.0 | `ag PM_RESUME` | 1.420 s | 17 Full methodology and more scenarios (case-insensitive, Unicode classes, many literals) live in [`benchsuite/`](benchsuite/README.md). *** ## FAQ ## **Why not just use ripgrep?** Honestly, you probably should if it already works for you. `sift` started as a learning project and grew a few features we wanted (the `--pre` cache, `.siftignore`). **Does it support Windows?** Yes. Paths are printed with `\` separators unless you pass `--path-separator /`. **Can I search inside `.zip` files?**\ Not directly. Use `--pre` with a small script that runs `unzip -p`. ## Contributing See [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md). Bug reports are welcome, especially ones that come with a reproducible case — `sift --debug` output helps a lot. Please run `cargo fmt` and `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings` before opening a PR. ## License Licensed under either of * Apache License, Version 2.0 ([LICENSE-APACHE][apache] or ) * MIT license ([LICENSE-MIT][mit] or http://opensource.org/licenses/MIT) at your option. Unless you say otherwise, any contribution you intentionally submit for inclusion in this project, as defined in the Apache-2.0 license, is dual licensed as above without any additional terms or conditions. [^name]: The name `sift` on crates.io belongs to an unrelated (and abandoned) 2016 project. We asked; no reply. [^bench]: AMD Ryzen 9 7950X, 64 GB DDR5, Samsung 990 Pro, Linux 6.8, ext4. Each command ran 10 times via `hyperfine --warmup 3`; the median is shown. [releases]: https://github.com/acme-tools/sift/releases "sift releases" [json-docs]: docs/json.md 'JSON output format' [apache]: LICENSE-APACHE [mit]: LICENSE-MIT (MIT license text)

[![Python versions](https://img.shields.io/pypi/pyversions/tidyframe.svg)](https://pypi.org/project/tidyframe/)
[![conda-forge](https://img.shields.io/conda/vn/conda-forge/tidyframe.svg)](https://anaconda.org/conda-forge/tidyframe)
[![codecov](https://codecov.io/gh/acme-data/tidyframe/branch/main/graph/badge.svg?token=Q8ZLX0R2KD)](https://codecov.io/gh/acme-data/tidyframe)
[![pre-commit.ci status](https://results.pre-commit.ci/badge/github/acme-data/tidyframe/main.svg)](https://results.pre-commit.ci/latest/github/acme-data/tidyframe/main)
[![Ruff](https://img.shields.io/endpoint?url=https://raw.githubusercontent.com/astral-sh/ruff/main/assets/badge/v2.json)](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff)
[![Downloads](https://static.pepy.tech/badge/tidyframe/month)](https://pepy.tech/project/tidyframe)

**tidyframe** is a small library of *verbs* for reshaping and cleaning pandas
and Polars DataFrames. It borrows the vocabulary of the tidyverse — `select`,
`mutate`, `pivot_longer`, `separate`, `nest` — and adds just enough sugar to make method
chains readable without hiding what pandas is doing underneath.

Installation
------------

Release builds are on PyPI and conda-forge:

```bash
pip install tidyframe
# with the optional Polars backend
pip install "tidyframe[polars]"
```

```bash
conda install -c conda-forge tidyframe
```

Or, if you've already moved to [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/):

    uv add tidyframe

tidyframe supports Python 3.9 – 3.13 and pandas ≥ 1.5. The Polars backend needs `polars>=0.20`.

## Quickstart

```python
import pandas as pd
import tidyframe as tf

raw = pd.read_csv("data/weather.csv")

tidy = (
    raw
    .pipe(tf.clean_names)                 # "Max Temp (°C)" -> max_temp_c
    .pipe(tf.pivot_longer, cols=tf.starts_with("d"), names_to="day", values_to="value")
    .pipe(tf.separate, "date", into=["year", "month"], sep="-")
    .pipe(tf.mutate, value=lambda d: d.value.astype("float32"))
    .dropna(subset=["value"])
)
```

The same verbs are available as a DataFrame accessor once the package is imported:

```pycon
>>> import tidyframe
>>> df = pd.DataFrame({"id": [1, 2], "x_2020": [3, 4], "x_2021": [5, 6]})
>>> df.tidy.pivot_longer(cols="x_*", names_to="year", names_prefix="x_")
   id  year  value
0   1  2020      3
1   2  2020      4
2   1  2021      5
3   2  2021      6
```

Why tidyframe?
--------------

Most of us have written the same five lines of `melt`/`rename`/`str.split` glue
more times than we'd like to admit. Each piece is easy; the combination is where
the bugs live — a forgotten `reset_index()`, a column name with a trailing space, a
`MultiIndex` nobody asked for.

tidyframe tries to make the *common* path boring. Every verb takes a DataFrame and returns
a new DataFrame, never mutates its input, and never leaves you with a MultiIndex
unless you explicitly ask for one with `keep_index=True`.

It is __not__ a replacement for pandas, and it doesn't try to be a full port of dplyr
either. If a verb would need more than ~200 lines to do the right
thing, it probably doesn't belong here.

| Feature                     | tidyframe | pandas only | siuba | pyjanitor |
|-----------------------------|:---------:|:-----------:|:-----:|:---------:|
| tidyverse-style verbs       | ✓         | ✗           | ✓     | partial   |
| pandas backend              | ✓         | ✓           | ✓     | ✓         |
| Polars backend              | ✓         | ✗           | ✗     | ✗         |
| lazy / SQL backends         | ✗         | ✗           | ✓     | ✗         |
| type hints (`py.typed`)     | ✓         | ✓           | ✗     | partial   |

Features
--------

* Column selection helpers
    * `starts_with`, `ends_with`, `contains`, `matches` (regex)
    * `where(dtype)` — e.g. `tf.where("number")`
        * accepts numpy dtypes, pandas extension dtypes or the strings `"number"`, `"string"`, `"datetime"`
    * negation with `~`, e.g. `~tf.starts_with("tmp_")`
* Reshaping
    * `pivot_longer` / `pivot_wider`
    * `separate`, `separate_rows`, `unite`
    * `nest` / `unnest` for list-columns
* Cleaning
    * `clean_names` (snake_case, strips accents: `Größe` → `grosse`, `Ångström` → `angstrom`)
    * `coalesce`, `na_if`, `replace_na`
        * all three respect pandas' nullable dtypes (`Int64`, `string[pyarrow]`)

> **Note**
> `tidyframe.compat` (the 0.x shims) was removed in 1.0. If you still import from
> it, pin `tidyframe<1.0` or follow the [migration notes][migrating].

### Configuration

There are only two global options, both set through `tf.options`:

`tf.options.copy_on_write`
:   Defaults to `True` on pandas ≥ 2.0. Set it to `False` to get the old behaviour
    (a little faster, a lot riskier).

`tf.options.backend`
:   `"pandas"` (default) or `"polars"`. Mostly useful in tests.

Development
-----------

```bash
git clone https://github.com/acme-data/tidyframe.git
cd tidyframe
python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -e ".[dev,polars]"
pre-commit install
pytest -n auto --cov=tidyframe
```

Docs are built with Sphinx (`make -C docs html`) and deployed to
<https://tidyframe.readthedocs.io> on every merge to `main`. 

___

## Citing

If tidyframe saved you time in a paper, a citation is appreciated (but never required):

```bibtex
@software{tidyframe,
  author    = {Okonkwo, Adaeze and Lindqvist, Henrik and {tidyframe contributors}},
  title     = {tidyframe: tidy data verbs for pandas and Polars},
  year      = {2024},
  publisher = {Zenodo},
  version   = {1.3.0},
  doi       = {10.5281/zenodo.10293847},
  url       = {https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.10293847}
}
```

## Related projects

- [siuba](https://github.com/machow/siuba) — dplyr-style verbs with SQL backends.
- [pyjanitor](https://pyjanitor-devs.github.io/pyjanitor/) — cleaning functions, several of which inspired ours.
- [pandas' own reshaping guide](https://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/stable/user_guide/reshaping.html#reshaping-by-melt) — worth re-reading, honestly.
- The tidyr vignette on [pivoting](https://tidyr.tidyverse.org/articles/pivot.html?q=pivot_longer#longer), which is where most of the naming comes from.[^naming]

License
-------

BSD-3-Clause, see [LICENSE](LICENSE). Copyright © 2021–2024 the tidyframe developers.

[^naming]: We deliberately kept `names_to` / `values_to` even though `var_name` / `value_name` would be more "pandas-y". Sharing tidyr's vocabulary makes translating R code much easier.

[migrating]: https://tidyframe.readthedocs.io/en/stable/migrating.html "Migrating from 0.x"
[docs]: https://tidyframe.readthedocs.io

# dotfiles #

my dotfiles. there are many like them, but these ones are mine :)

Managed with [GNU Stow](https://www.gnu.org/software/stow/) because I tried chezmoi
and yadm and the bare-repo-with-an-alias trick and kept coming back to the simplest thing.
Mostly Arch on the desktop, macOS on the work laptop, the
occasional Debian VPS. Things are *supposed* to work on all three but no
promises — PRs welcome, issues less so.

![screenshot of my desktop](img/desktop-2024.png "sway + waybar + foot, gruvbox-ish")

***

## what's in here ##

* `zsh/` — zshrc, aliases, a handful of functions
* `fish/` — I keep switching back and forth, don't judge
+ `nvim/` — neovim config, lua, lazy.nvim
+ `tmux/`
* `git/` — gitconfig with delta as the pager, global gitignore
* `sway/`, `waybar/`, `foot/`, `mako/` (linux only)
* `bin/` — random scripts. some of them are terrible.
    * `bin/wttr` — weather in the terminal
    * `bin/gc-branches` — deletes merged branches, asks first
    + `bin/ocr-screenshot` — grim + slurp + tesseract, surprisingly useful

## install ##

1) clone it somewhere. I use `~/.dotfiles`:

        git clone --recursive https://github.com/jdoe/dotfiles.git ~/.dotfiles

2) install stow (`pacman -S stow` / `brew install stow` / `apt install stow`)
3) stow whatever you want:

```sh
cd ~/.dotfiles
stow -v zsh git nvim tmux
# linux only
stow -v sway waybar foot mako
```

4) open nvim once and let lazy.nvim do its thing. it'll complain about a missing
   `stylua` — ignore it or `cargo install stylua`

thats it. there's also a `bootstrap.sh` that does all of the above *and* installs
packages, but read it first, it __will__ overwrite things.

    curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jdoe/dotfiles/main/bootstrap.sh | less
    # if you're brave:
    # curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jdoe/dotfiles/main/bootstrap.sh | sh

___

## shell

zsh with no framework (oh-my-zsh made startup take 600ms, now it's ~40ms).
the prompt is [starship](https://starship.rs). history is shared between sessions,
deduped, and 100k lines long because disk is cheap.

some aliases I actually use:

```sh
alias g='git'
alias gs='git status -sb'
alias ll='eza -lah --git --group-directories-first'
alias k='kubectl'
alias please='sudo $(fc -ln -1)'   # :^)
```

the fish config is roughly equivalent:


# acme-lakehouse pipelines

Batch ELT for the Acme analytics lakehouse: **Airflow** orchestrates, **Spark** does the heavy lifting on
raw event data, and **dbt** builds the modelled layers in the warehouse. This repo
holds the DAGs, the Spark jobs, the dbt project and the local dev setup.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> Production runs on MWAA (Airflow 2.8) in `eu-west-1`. Nothing in this README
> touches production — the local stack uses MinIO and a throwaway Postgres.

## Architecture

```text
                +-------------------+        +-------------------+
  app events -->|  Kinesis Firehose |------->|  s3://acme-raw/   |
                +-------------------+        +---------+---------+
                                                       |
                                     (hourly) Airflow  |  spark-submit
                                                       v
+-------------+   dbt run    +----------------+   +----+--------------+
| BI / Looker |<-------------|  Snowflake     |<--|  s3://acme-stage/ |
+-------------+              |  (marts, core) |   |  (parquet, delta) |
                             +----------------+   +-------------------+
```

Same thing as a mermaid diagram, for people reading this on GitHub:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[App events] -->|Firehose| B[(S3 raw)]
    B -->|spark: sessionize| C[(S3 stage)]
    C -->|COPY INTO| D[(Snowflake RAW)]
    D -->|dbt| E[core models]
    E -->|dbt| F[marts]
    F --> G{{Looker}}
```

Each DAG follows the same shape: `sensor → spark job(s) → load → dbt build → data tests → notify`. Spark jobs are idempotent per partition (they overwrite `dt=YYYY-MM-DD/hr=HH` partitions), so re-running a task is always safe; dbt models are incremental with `unique_key` set, which means a three-day backfill costs roughly three days of compute rather than a full refresh — unless someone changed a model's schema, in which case CI will tell you to run with `--full-refresh`, and you should coordinate in #data-eng before doing that because `fct_sessions` is about 4 TB and a full refresh takes most of a working day on an XL warehouse.

## Configuration

All configuration comes from environment variables (locally from `.env`, on MWAA from Secrets Manager via the `aws_secrets` backend).

| Variable | Required | Default | Description |
|----------|:--------:|---------|-------------|
| `LAKE_RAW_BUCKET` | yes | — | Bucket with raw Firehose output. Locally this is `acme-raw` in MinIO. |
| `LAKE_STAGE_BUCKET` | yes | — | Where Spark writes Delta tables, partitioned by `dt` and `hr`. Must be in the same region as the EMR cluster or you'll pay cross-region transfer for every single job, which is how we got a surprisingly large bill in March 2023. |
| `SPARK_MASTER` | no | `local[*]` | Spark master URL. `yarn` on EMR; `local[4]` if your laptop fans start screaming. |
| `SNOWFLAKE_ACCOUNT` | yes | — | e.g. `acme-eu1`. |
| `SNOWFLAKE_ROLE` | no | `TRANSFORMER` | Role used by dbt; needs `USAGE` on the warehouse and `OWNERSHIP` on the target schemas. |
| `DBT_TARGET` | no | `dev` | One of `dev`, `ci`, `prod`. `prod` refuses to run from a laptop (checked in `profiles.yml` via `env_var('AIRFLOW_CTX_DAG_ID', '')`). |
| `SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL` | no | *empty* | If set, failures are posted to #data-alerts. |
| `PIPELINE_LOOKBACK_HOURS` | no | `3` | How many hours each hourly run reprocesses to catch late-arriving events. |

## Running locally

1. Copy the env template and fill in your Snowflake dev credentials:

    ```bash
    cp .env.example .env
    $EDITOR .env
    ```

2. Start the stack (Airflow webserver + scheduler, MinIO, Postgres, a Spark master and one worker):

    ```bash
    docker compose up -d --build
    docker compose ps
    ```

    - Airflow UI: http://localhost:8080 (user `airflow`, password `airflow`)
    - MinIO console: http://localhost:9001
    - Spark UI: http://localhost:8081
        - the worker UI is on 8082 but you'll rarely need it

3. Seed MinIO with a day of sample events:

    ```bash
    python scripts/seed_minio.py \
        --bucket acme-raw \
        --date 2024-05-01 \
        --events 250000 \
        --seed 42
    ```

4. Trigger a DAG run for that date:

    ```bash
    docker compose exec airflow-scheduler \
      airflow dags trigger events_hourly \
        --conf '{"start": "2024-05-01T00:00:00", "end": "2024-05-01T23:00:00"}'
    ```

5. Run dbt against your dev schema:
    * `make dbt-build` — builds everything downstream of `stg_events`
    * `make dbt-build SELECT=+fct_sessions` — just one model and its parents
    * `make dbt-docs` — serves the docs on :8085

> [!WARNING]
> The local Spark worker has 4 GB of memory. Things that **will** blow up:
> - running `sessions_backfill` for more than ~2 days of data
> - `--conf spark.sql.shuffle.partitions=2000` (copied from the EMR config)
> - the `identity_graph` job, at all — it needs the EMR cluster

6. When you're done, tear everything down (add `-v` to also drop the MinIO and Postgres volumes):

    ```bash
    docker compose down
    ```

## Project layout

```
.
├── dags/                  # one file per DAG, plus dags/common/
├── spark_jobs/
│   ├── sessionize.py
│   ├── dedupe_events.py
│   └── identity_graph/    # scala, built separately (see its README)
├── dbt/
│   ├── models/{staging,core,marts}/
│   ├── macros/
│   └── tests/
├── docker/                # Dockerfiles for local airflow & spark
├── scripts/
└── tests/                 # pytest: DAG integrity + spark unit tests
```

## DAGs

DAG | Schedule | Owner | SLA
--- | --- | --- | ---
`events_hourly` | `15 * * * *` | @data-eng | 45 min
`sessions_daily` | `0 3 * * *` | @data-eng | 2 h
`identity_graph_weekly` | `0 5 * * 1` | @growth-data | 6 h
`gdpr_erasure` | `@daily` | @privacy | 24 h[^gdpr]

#### Last quarter

|DAG|runs|failures|p95 duration|
|-|-|-|-|
|events_hourly|2184|11|19m|
|sessions_daily| 91 | 2 | 1h 12m |
|identity_graph_weekly|13|3|4h 51m|

Most `events_hourly` failures were Firehose delivering a partition late, which the next run picks up anyway thanks to the lookback window; the `identity_graph_weekly` failures were all spot-instance interruptions on EMR, which we've since mitigated by moving the core nodes to on-demand.[^spot]

## Testing

```bash
make test            # pytest, ~2 min
make lint            # ruff + sqlfluff
make dag-integrity   # imports every DAG, fails on cycles or import errors
```

CI runs the same targets plus `dbt build --target ci` against a zero-copy clone of prod (see [the CI docs][ci-docs]).

## Troubleshooting

**`Py4JJavaError ... OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space`** — your local worker is too small; see the warning above.

**dbt says `Compilation Error ... depends on a node named 'stg_events__v2' which was not found`** — you're on an old branch. `git pull` and run `make dbt-deps`.

**DAG doesn't show up in the UI** — check `docker compose logs airflow-scheduler | grep -i error`. Nine times out of ten it's an import error in `dags/common/`, and every DAG that imports it silently disappears.

## Owners

Maintained by the Data Engineering team (#data-eng on Slack). The on-call rotation is in [PagerDuty][pd];
runbooks live in [Confluence](https://acme.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/DATA/pages/2287435777/Pipeline+Runbooks?focusedCommentId=99812#comments).

[^gdpr]: The legal requirement is 30 days from the request; 24 h is our internal target.
[^spot]: See the postmortem: https://acme.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/DATA/pages/2301122561

[ci-docs]: docs/ci.md
[pd]: https://acme.pagerduty.com/schedules#PX7Q2LM "Data on-call"

# ledgerd #

[![Go Report Card](https://goreportcard.com/badge/github.com/acme-fin/ledgerd)](https://goreportcard.com/report/github.com/acme-fin/ledgerd) [![Go Reference](https://pkg.go.dev/badge/github.com/acme-fin/ledgerd.svg)](https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/acme-fin/ledgerd) [![Docker Pulls](https://img.shields.io/docker/pulls/acmefin/ledgerd.svg)](https://hub.docker.com/r/acmefin/ledgerd)
[![codecov](https://codecov.io/gh/acme-fin/ledgerd/branch/main/graph/badge.svg)](https://codecov.io/gh/acme-fin/ledgerd)
[![Release](https://img.shields.io/github/v/release/acme-fin/ledgerd?sort=semver)](https://github.com/acme-fin/ledgerd/releases/latest)

`ledgerd` is a small double-entry ledger service. It stores accounts and
immutable transactions in PostgreSQL, enforces that every transaction balances,
and exposes a JSON/HTTP API plus a gRPC API for internal callers.

It has been the system of record for balances at Acme Pay since 2022 and handles
roughly 3k transactions per second at peak.

## Quick start ##

Requirements: Go 1.22+, Docker (for Postgres), `make`.

```sh
git clone https://github.com/acme-fin/ledgerd.git && cd ledgerd
make dev-db      # starts postgres:16 on :5433
make migrate
make run
```

### Makefile targets

| Target | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `make build` | Builds `./bin/ledgerd` with `-trimpath` and version info from `git describe` |
| `make test` | Unit tests with `-race` |
| `make test-integration` | Spins up Postgres via testcontainers; needs Docker |
| `make lint` | `golangci-lint run` using `.golangci.yml` |
| `make migrate` / `make migrate-down` | Applies / rolls back one migration with `goose` |
| `make gen` | Regenerates protobuf (`buf generate`) and the sqlc code |
| `make docker` | Builds the image `acmefin/ledgerd:dev` |

## API

All endpoints live under `/v1`; requests and responses are JSON. Amounts are **integers in minor units** (cents), never floats.

Method | Path | Description
:----- | :--- | :----------
`POST` | `/v1/accounts` | Create an account
`GET` | `/v1/accounts/{id}` | Fetch an account with its current balance
`GET` | `/v1/accounts/{id}/entries` | List entries, newest first; cursor-paginated
`POST` | `/v1/transactions` | Post a balanced transaction (idempotent via `Idempotency-Key`)
`GET` | `/v1/transactions/{id}` | Fetch a transaction and its entries
`POST` | `/v1/transactions/{id}/reverse` | Create a reversing transaction
`GET` | `/healthz`, `/readyz` | Liveness / readiness

#### Examples

1. Create two accounts:
   ```sh
   curl -s -X POST localhost:8080/v1/accounts \
     -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
     -d '{"name": "cash", "currency": "EUR", "normal_balance": "debit"}'
   ```
2. Post a transaction moving €12.50 from `cash` to `revenue`:

   ```sh
   curl -s -X POST localhost:8080/v1/transactions \
     -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
     -H 'Idempotency-Key: 6f1c2a9e-0d7b-4f3e-9a51-2b8f4c7d1e03' \
     -d @- <<'EOF'
   {
     "description": "Order #10442",
     "entries": [
       {"account_id": "acc_01HV9ZK3", "direction": "credit", "amount": 1250},
       {"account_id": "acc_01HV9YQ7", "direction": "debit",  "amount": 1250}
     ]
   }
   EOF
   ```

   A transaction whose debits and credits don't sum to zero is rejected with `422` and `{"error": "unbalanced_transaction"}`.

3. Read the balance back

   ```console
   $ curl -s localhost:8080/v1/accounts/acc_01HV9YQ7 | jq .balance
   1250
   ```

## Configuration ##

Configuration comes from environment variables only — there is no config file, on purpose.

`LEDGERD_PORT`
:   The port the HTTP server listens on. Default `8080`.

`LEDGERD_GRPC_PORT`
:   Port for the gRPC server. Default `9090`. Set to `0` to disable gRPC entirely.

`LEDGERD_DATABASE_URL`
:   PostgreSQL connection string, e.g.
    `postgres://ledgerd:secret@localhost:5433/ledgerd?sslmode=disable`.
    **Required.**

`LEDGERD_MAX_CONNS`
:   Maximum size of the `pgxpool` pool. Default `20`.

`LEDGERD_LOG_LEVEL`
:   `debug`, `info` (default), `warn` or `error`.

`LEDGERD_OTEL_ENDPOINT`
:   OTLP/gRPC endpoint for traces, e.g. `otel-collector:4317`. Tracing is off when unset.

> [!TIP]
> In Kubernetes, keep `LEDGERD_DATABASE_URL` in a Secret and reference it with `envFrom`; the Helm chart in
> [`deploy/helm`](deploy/helm) already does this.

## Docker

~~~dockerfile
FROM golang:1.22-alpine AS build
WORKDIR /src
COPY go.mod go.sum ./
RUN go mod download
COPY . .
ARG VERSION=dev
RUN CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -trimpath -ldflags="-s -w -X main.version=${VERSION}" -o /out/ledgerd ./cmd/ledgerd

FROM gcr.io/distroless/static-debian12:nonroot
COPY --from=build /out/ledgerd /ledgerd
EXPOSE 8080 9090
USER nonroot:nonroot
ENTRYPOINT ["/ledgerd"]
~~~

Pre-built images are pushed to Docker Hub as `acmefin/ledgerd:<version>` and `:latest` on every release.

## Design notes #

A few decisions that come up in every other code review:

> Why not store the balance as a column and update it in place?
>
> > Because then the balance and the entries can disagree, and when they do you
> > have no way of knowing which one is right. We compute balances from entries and
> > cache them in `account_balances`, which is rebuilt nightly and compared.
>
> — from the original design doc, 2021

- Transactions are **immutable**. Corrections are new, reversing transactions.
- Every write runs at `SERIALIZABLE` isolation; we retry on SQLSTATE `40001` up to 5 times with jitter.
- IDs are ULIDs with a type prefix (`acc_`, `txn_`, `ent_`) so they sort by time and you can tell what something is from a log line.

## Observability

Prometheus metrics are exposed on `:8080/metrics`:

- `ledgerd_http_requests_total{route,method,code}`
- `ledgerd_http_request_duration_seconds` (histogram)
- `ledgerd_transactions_posted_total{currency}`
- `ledgerd_tx_retries_total` — serialization failures that were retried
    - if this climbs above ~1% of `ledgerd_transactions_posted_total`, something is hot-spotting a single account
- `ledgerd_db_pool_acquired_conns` / `ledgerd_db_pool_idle_conns`

Logs are structured JSON (`log/slog`), one line per request, with a `trace_id` when tracing is enabled.

## Contributing ##

Run `make lint test` before pushing. Commit messages follow [Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/en/v1.0.0/#summary).
Changes to the database schema need a migration **and** a note in `docs/schema-changes.md`.

# Awesome Static Site Generators [![Awesome](https://awesome.re/badge.svg)](https://awesome.re)

> A curated list of static site generators, themes, hosting platforms and tooling — the
good stuff, not every abandoned weekend project on GitHub.

Static site generators (SSGs) take plain files — usually Markdown plus some templates — and turn them into a folder of HTML you can host anywhere. This list focuses on generators that are actively maintained (a release or meaningful commit in the last 12 months), documented well enough that a newcomer can ship something in an afternoon, and used in production by someone other than their author. Star badges are there for a rough sense of popularity, not quality; projects marked with \* are documentation-oriented.

## Contents

- [Generators](#generators)
  - [JavaScript / TypeScript](#javascript--typescript)
  - [Go](#go)
  - [Python](#python)
  - [Ruby](#ruby)
  - [Rust](#rust)
  - [Other languages](#other-languages)
- [Documentation-focused](#documentation-focused)
- [Headless CMS](#headless-cms)
- [Hosting](#hosting)
- [Tooling](#tooling)
  - [Images](#images)
  - [Search](#search)
- [Articles & talks](#articles--talks)
- [Contributing](#contributing)

## Generators

### JavaScript / TypeScript

- [Astro](https://astro.build) - Content-focused framework with islands architecture; ships zero JS by default. ![GitHub stars](https://img.shields.io/github/stars/withastro/astro?style=social)
- [Eleventy (11ty)](https://www.11ty.dev) - Simple and flexible, supports ten template languages at once. ![GitHub stars](https://img.shields.io/github/stars/11ty/eleventy?style=social)
    - [11ty starter projects](https://www.11ty.dev/docs/starter/) - Community-maintained list of starters, sortable by build performance.
    - [eleventy-plugin-vite](https://github.com/11ty/eleventy-plugin-vite) - Use Vite as the dev server and bundler.
- [Gatsby](https://www.gatsbyjs.com) - React-based with a GraphQL data layer. Development has slowed down considerably over the last couple of years, but there is a huge plugin ecosystem and a lot of existing sites, so you will keep running into it at work whether you like it or not.
- [Next.js](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/building-your-application/deploying/static-exports) - With `output: 'export'`, as long as you avoid server-only features.
- [VitePress](https://vitepress.dev) - Vue-powered and Vite-based. \*
- [Hexo](https://hexo.io) - Blog-focused, popular in the Chinese-speaking community (中文文档很完善).
- [Docusaurus][docusaurus] - See [Documentation-focused](#documentation-focused).

### Go

* [Hugo][hugo] - The fast one. A single binary, no dependencies, builds thousands of pages per second. ![GitHub stars](https://img.shields.io/github/stars/gohugoio/hugo?style=social)
    * [Hugo Themes](https://themes.gohugo.io/) - Official theme directory.
    * [Hugo Modules](https://gohugo.io/hugo-modules/) - Go-modules-based system for themes and shared content.
    * [Blowfish](https://blowfish.page) - Tailwind-based theme with a lot of knobs.
* [Hugo Book theme](https://github.com/alex-shpak/hugo-book) - Docs theme, no JS required. \*

### Python

- [Pelican](https://getpelican.com) - Mature, Jinja2 templates, reStructuredText or Markdown.
- [MkDocs][mkdocs] - Project documentation with Markdown. \*
    - [Material for MkDocs](https://squidfunk.github.io/mkdocs-material/) - The theme most people actually mean when they say "MkDocs".
    - [mkdocstrings](https://mkdocstrings.github.io/) - API docs from docstrings.
- [Sphinx](https://www.sphinx-doc.org) - The documentation tool behind docs.python.org; reST first, Markdown via MyST. \*
- [Nikola](https://getnikola.com) - Incremental builds, Jupyter notebooks as posts.
- [Lektor](https://www.getlektor.com) - SSG with an admin UI, from the author of Flask.

### Ruby

* [Jekyll] - The original GitHub Pages generator. Still everywhere.
* [Bridgetown](https://www.bridgetownrb.com) - A modern Jekyll fork with esbuild and Ruby components.
* [Middleman](https://middlemanapp.com) - Rails-like, Sprockets-era but still maintained.
* [Nanoc](https://nanoc.app) - Flexible, rule-based; great for unusual site structures.

### Rust

- [Zola][] - Single binary, Tera templates, built-in Sass, search index and syntax highlighting. ![GitHub stars](https://img.shields.io/github/stars/getzola/zola?style=social)
- [mdBook](https://rust-lang.github.io/mdBook/) - Create books from Markdown; used for The Rust Programming Language. \*
- [Cobalt](https://cobalt-org.github.io) - Liquid templates, Jekyll-like conventions.

### Other languages

- [Hakyll](https://jaspervdj.be/hakyll/) (Haskell) - A library rather than a framework; you write your site generator in Haskell.
- [Franklin.jl](https://franklinjl.org) (Julia) - Good LaTeX/math support, can evaluate Julia code blocks.
- [Quarto](https://quarto.org) (multi-language) - Scientific and technical publishing with R, Python, Julia and Observable.
- [soupault](https://soupault.app) (OCaml) - Works on the HTML element tree instead of templates.
- [Pollen](https://docs.racket-lang.org/pollen/) (Racket) - "Book is a program". Unusual, beautiful output.

## Documentation-focused

| Tool | Language | Versioned docs | i18n | Search |
|------|----------|:--------------:|:----:|--------|
| [Docusaurus][docusaurus] | React | ✓ | ✓ | Algolia / local plugins |
| [Material for MkDocs](https://squidfunk.github.io/mkdocs-material/) | Python | via `mike` | ✓ | built-in (lunr) |
| [Starlight](https://starlight.astro.build) | Astro | ✗ | ✓ | Pagefind |
| [VitePress](https://vitepress.dev) | Vue | ✗ | ✓ | local / Algolia |
| [mdBook](https://rust-lang.github.io/mdBook/) | Rust | ✗ | ✗ | built-in |

## Headless CMS

- [Decap CMS](https://decapcms.org) - Git-based, formerly Netlify CMS. Config lives in a YAML file next to your content.
- [TinaCMS](https://tina.io) - Git-backed with visual editing; GraphQL API over your Markdown.
- [Sanity](https://www.sanity.io) - Hosted content lake, very customizable studio.
- [Strapi](https://strapi.io) - Self-hosted Node.js CMS with REST and GraphQL.

## Hosting

- [Cloudflare Pages](https://pages.cloudflare.com) - Generous free tier, preview deployments.
- [GitHub Pages](https://pages.github.com) - Free for public repos; Actions-based builds for any generator.
- [GitLab Pages](https://docs.gitlab.com/ee/user/project/pages/) - Same idea, works with self-hosted GitLab.
- [Netlify](https://www.netlify.com) - Pioneered the "push to deploy" workflow; forms, functions, redirects.
- [Neocities](https://neocities.org) - Free hosting for personal sites, very GeoCities-spirited.

## Tooling

### Images

- [sharp](https://sharp.pixelplumbing.com) - Fast Node.js image processing (libvips).
- [imgproxy](https://imgproxy.net) - Resize images on the fly; useful when your build would otherwise generate 40 variants per photo.

### Search

- [Pagefind](https://pagefind.app) - Static search index that loads only the chunks it needs. Works with any generator.
- [Lunr.js](https://lunrjs.com) - Small full-text search for the browser.
- [Fuse.js](https://www.fusejs.io) - Fuzzy search, good for small sites.

# acme/platform Monorepo for Acme's customer-facing web platform: the Next.js storefront, the admin dashboard, shared UI components, and a handful of internal libraries. Everything is TypeScript, managed with **pnpm workspaces** and **Turborepo**. ## Packages | Package | Version | Description | |:--------|:-------:|:------------| | [`apps/storefront`](apps/storefront) | — | Public storefront (Next.js 14, App Router) | | [`apps/admin`](apps/admin) | — | Internal admin dashboard (Vite + React) | | [`@acme/ui`](packages/ui) | ![npm](https://img.shields.io/npm/v/@acme/ui?label=&color=0b7285) | Design-system components; Storybook at | | [`@acme/config-eslint`](packages/config-eslint) | ![npm](https://img.shields.io/npm/v/@acme/config-eslint?label=) | Shared ESLint flat config | | [`@acme/config-ts`](packages/config-ts) | ![npm](https://img.shields.io/npm/v/@acme/config-ts?label=) | `tsconfig` bases (`base.json`, `nextjs.json`, `library.json`) | | [`@acme/api-client`](packages/api-client) | ![npm](https://img.shields.io/npm/v/@acme/api-client?label=) | Typed client generated from the OpenAPI spec in `apis/commerce.yaml` | | [`@acme/utils`](packages/utils) | `0.0.0` (private) | Grab-bag of helpers. Please don't add more stuff here 🙃 | ## Repository structure ``` platform/ ├── apps/ │ ├── admin/ │ └── storefront/ ├── packages/ │ ├── api-client/ │ ├── config-eslint/ │ ├── config-ts/ │ ├── ui/ │ └── utils/ ├── apis/ # OpenAPI specs (source of truth for api-client) ├── tooling/ │ └── scripts/ ├── turbo.json ├── pnpm-workspace.yaml └── package.json ``` ## Getting started You need Node 20 (see `.nvmrc`) and pnpm 9. The easiest way to get the right pnpm is Corepack: ```bash corepack enable pnpm install ``` > [!NOTE] > `pnpm install` runs a `postinstall` that generates `packages/api-client/src/gen/`. If that > step fails you're probably missing Java (needed by `openapi-generator-cli`) — see Troubleshooting below. ### Common commands ```bash pnpm dev # everything, in parallel pnpm -F storefront dev # just the storefront pnpm -F "@acme/ui" storybook pnpm build # turbo build, cached pnpm lint && pnpm typecheck pnpm test -- --watch # vitest pnpm -F admin add react-hook-form # add a dependency to one workspace pnpm -w add -D prettier # ...or to the root ``` Turbo caches task outputs locally in `node_modules/.cache/turbo` and remotely (Vercel Remote Cache) when `TURBO_TOKEN` is set, so the second `pnpm build` on an unchanged tree should finish in well under a second; if it doesn't, something in your environment is leaking into the task hash — usually an env var that isn't listed in `turbo.json` under `globalEnv` or the task's `env`, and `pnpm turbo run build --dry=json | jq '.tasks[].environmentVariables'` will tell you which one. To bypass the cache entirely, run `pnpm build --force`. > [!TIP] > Filter by what changed since `main` with `pnpm turbo run test --filter=...[origin/main]` — > that's what CI does. ## Conventions - Workspace names - apps: plain names (`storefront`, `admin`) - libraries: `@acme/*`, published to GitHub Packages - except `@acme/utils`, which is private and never published - Imports - never import from another package's `src/`; use its public entry point - inside a package, use the `#` subpath imports defined in its `package.json` - e.g. `import { cn } from "#lib/cn"` - Docs: when you need to show a template literal in Markdown, wrap it in double backticks, like `` `Hello ${name}` ``. > [!IMPORTANT] > Changes to anything in `packages/` need a changeset: run `pnpm changeset` and commit the generated file. > CI fails without one. A changeset is just a Markdown file with front matter: ````md --- "@acme/ui": minor "@acme/api-client": patch --- Add `` component. Usage: ```tsx ``` ```` ## Releasing Libraries are versioned with [Changesets](https://github.com/changesets/changesets). Apps are deployed continuously from `main` and aren't versioned. Release checklist (for whoever is on release duty that week): - [ ] Merge the "Version Packages" PR opened by the changesets bot - [ ] double-check that the generated CHANGELOG entries read well - [ ] confirm no `major` bump snuck in for `@acme/ui` without an RFC - [ ] Wait for the `release` workflow to publish to GitHub Packages - [ ] Bump `@acme/ui` in the storefront and admin (Renovate usually does this within the hour) - [x] ~~Post in #frontend~~ — automated by the workflow now - [ ] Redeploy Storybook if it didn't trigger on its own > [!CAUTION] > Never run `pnpm publish` locally. The workflow publishes with provenance and a scoped token; a local publish skips both and has, in the past, shipped a package with a `.env` file in it. > > If you think you need a manual publish, talk to the platform leads first. There is almost always another way.
Troubleshooting 1. **`ERR_PNPM_BAD_PM_VERSION`** — you're using a globally installed pnpm. Run ```bash npm uninstall -g pnpm corepack enable ``` 2. **`openapi-generator-cli: java: command not found`** — install a JRE: ```bash brew install --cask temurin@21 # macOS sudo apt install -y openjdk-21-jre-headless # Debian/Ubuntu ``` 3. **Turbo keeps replaying a stale build** Delete the local cache and rebuild: ```bash rm -rf node_modules/.cache/turbo pnpm build --force ``` 4. **Storybook fails with `Cannot find module '@acme/config-ts/base.json'`** after switching branches: run `pnpm install` again, the workspace links are stale.
## CI GitHub Actions, see `.github/workflows/`. The main workflow runs `lint`, `typecheck`, `test` and `build` for affected packages only.[^affected] Vercel creates preview deployments for both apps on every PR. ## Ownership `CODEOWNERS` maps directories to teams. Roughly: * `apps/storefront` — web-storefront * `apps/admin` — backoffice * `packages/ui` — design-systems * everything else — platform [^affected]: "Affected" is computed by Turborepo against the merge base with `main`. Changes to the root `package.json`, `pnpm-lock.yaml` or `turbo.json` mark *everything* as affected. That's intentional, if annoying: a lockfile change can change the behaviour of any package, and we'd rather run the full suite than find out in production.

# Changelog
All notable changes to `acme-sdk` will be documented in this file.

The format is based on [Keep a Changelog](https://keepachangelog.com/en/1.1.0/),
and this project adheres to [Semantic Versioning](https://semver.org/spec/v2.0.0.html).
The Python and TypeScript SDKs share version numbers; entries tagged *(py)* or *(ts)* apply to only one of them.

## [Unreleased]
### Added
- `Client.with_options()` for per-request overrides of `timeout` and `max_retries` ([#1482](https://github.com/acme/acme-sdk/pull/1482))
- *(ts)* The ESM build is now tree-shakeable (`"sideEffects": false` in `package.json`)

### Changed
- Default `max_retries` raised from 2 to 3. Retries still only happen on
  connection errors, `408`, `409`, `429` and `5xx` responses.

## [3.2.0] - 2024-05-14
### Added
- Streaming helpers: `client.events.stream()` returns an async iterator of typed events.
  - supports `Last-Event-ID` resumption via `stream(resume_from=...)`
  - emits a `heartbeat` event every 15s, which is filtered out unless `include_heartbeats=True`
- `Webhook.verify()` accepts a list of secrets, so you can rotate without downtime ([#1440](https://github.com/acme/acme-sdk/issues/1440))
- *(py)* Type stubs for `acme_sdk.types.webhooks`

### Fixed
- Pagination iterators no longer request one extra, empty page when `has_more` is
false on the last page ([#1451](https://github.com/acme/acme-sdk/issues/1451))
- `AcmeError.__str__` included the request body, which could leak card numbers into logs. It now only includes the request ID. 

### Security
- Raised the `urllib3` lower bound to `>=2.2.2` (CVE-2024-37891).

## [3.1.1] - 2024-04-02
### Fixed
- *(ts)* A `fetch` polyfill was accidentally bundled into the Node 18+ build, adding ~40 kB.
- Retries ignored the `Retry-After` header when it was given as an HTTP date rather than as seconds.

## [3.1.0] - 2024-03-11
### Added
- `client.invoices.finalize()` and `client.invoices.void()`
- Idempotency keys are generated automatically for `POST` requests unless you pass `idempotency_key=None`
    - the generated key is a UUIDv4 and is logged at `DEBUG`
    - keys you pass explicitly are never modified
### Deprecated
- `client.invoices.close()` — use `finalize()` instead; `close()` will be removed in 4.0
### Fixed
- Timeouts passed as `httpx.Timeout` objects were silently replaced by the default ([#1398](https://github.com/acme/acme-sdk/issues/1398))

## [3.0.0] - 2024-01-22
### Changed
- **BREAKING:** The minimum Python version is now 3.9; the minimum Node version is 18.
- **BREAKING:** All list methods return auto-paginating iterators instead of a
  `Page` object. To get the old behaviour, call `.page()`:
  ```python
  page = client.customers.list(limit=50).page()
  for customer in page.data:
      ...
  ```
- **BREAKING:** Renamed `AcmeAPIError` → `APIError` and `AcmeConnectionError` → `APIConnectionError`.
  The old names remain as aliases until 4.0 and emit a `DeprecationWarning`.
- Response objects are now Pydantic v2 models *(py)* / readonly interfaces *(ts)*.

### Removed
- **BREAKING:** the `acme_sdk.legacy` module and the `api_base` global.
- Support for the `Acme-Version: 2021-06-01` header.

### Fixed
- Thread-safety issue when sharing one `Client` between threads with HTTP/2 enabled ([#1301](https://github.com/acme/acme-sdk/issues/1301), thanks @mkowalski)

## [2.6.0] - 2023-11-08
### Added
- `client.refunds` resource
- `ACME_LOG=debug` environment variable that logs requests and responses (with `Authorization` redacted)
### Changed
- The `User-Agent` now includes the runtime, e.g. `acme-sdk-python/2.6.0 CPython/3.12.0`

## [2.5.2] - 2023-10-17
### Fixed
- The `py.typed` marker was missing from the wheel. 

## [2.5.1] - 2023-10-03
### Fixed
- Regression in 2.5.0: `customer.metadata` was `None` instead of `{}` when empty.
### Security
- Don't follow redirects to a different host when an `Authorization` header is set.

## [2.5.0] - 2023-09-19
### Added
- Async client (`AsyncClient`) *(py)*
  - same surface as `Client`; every method is a coroutine
  - uses `httpx.AsyncClient` under the hood, pass your own via `http_client=`
      - handy for sharing a connection pool with the rest of your app
- Request/response hooks: `on_request`, `on_response`

## [2.4.0] - 2023-08-01
### Added
- Support for the `2023-07-15` API version.
### Changed
- Errors expose `.request_id` and `.status_code` as attributes instead of only in the message.
### Fixed
- Duplicate webhook deliveries when two events had the same `created` timestamp — this
  is the proper fix for the issue that 2.3.1 tried to address.

## [2.3.1] - 2023-07-12 [YANKED]
### Fixed
- Attempted fix for duplicate webhook deliveries. Yanked because it dropped
  events with identical timestamps; upgrade to 2.4.0.

## [2.3.0] - 2023-06-20
### Added
- Webhook signature verification helpers (`Webhook.construct_event`).
### Fixed
- Unicode in metadata values (e.g. `"café"`, `"東京"`) was double-encoded ([#842](https://github.com/acme/acme-sdk/issues/842))

## [2.2.0] - 2023-04-27
### Added
- `client.customers.search(query=...)` using the new search endpoint.
### Deprecated
- `client.customers.list(email=...)`. Use `search(query="email:'a@example.com'")`.

## [2.0.0] - 2023-02-06
### Changed
- **BREAKING:** A new `Client` class replaces the module-level functions:
  ```diff
  - import acme_sdk
  - acme_sdk.api_key = "sk_test_..."
  - acme_sdk.Customer.create(email="a@example.com")
  + from acme_sdk import Client
  + client = Client(api_key="sk_test_...")
  + client.customers.create(email="a@example.com")
  ```
- Switched the HTTP layer from `requests` to `httpx`.
### Removed
- Python 3.6 and 3.7 support.

## [1.2.0] - 2022-09-14
### Added
- `expand=` parameter on all retrieve methods.
- Automatic retries with exponential backoff (off by default; enable with `max_retries=2`).

## [1.1.0] - 2022-05-30
### Added
- Customers and invoices resources.
### Fixed
- Typo in `Charge.captured_at` (was `captued_at`). The old name still works but is undocumented.

## [1.0.0] - 2022-03-01
### Added
- First stable release. 🎉

## [0.9.0] - 2021-12-02
### Added
- Release candidate for 1.0; charges and payment intents only.

## Adding a new package

1. Copy the template:
   ```bash
   cp -r tooling/templates/library packages/my-lib
   ```
1. Rename it in `packages/my-lib/package.json` (`"name": "@acme/my-lib"`) and set `"private": true` until it's ready to publish.
1. Run `pnpm install` from the root so the workspace link is created.
1. Add the package to the **Packages** table above and to `CODEOWNERS`.

## Environment variables

Var | Used by | Notes
--- | --- | ---
`NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL` | storefront | defaults to `https://api.acme.dev` in production
`VITE_API_URL` | admin | same as above, Vite flavour
`TURBO_TOKEN` / `TURBO_TEAM` | CI, optional locally | enables the remote cache
`SENTRY_AUTH_TOKEN` | build | uploads source maps; builds work fine without it

Local overrides go in `.env.local` files, which are git-ignored. Never commit real tokens — `gitleaks` runs in a pre-commit hook and in CI.
